subject: VertexLabs - Tailored reserved/burst SKU architecture & memory safety plan

Subject: VertexLabs - Tailored reserved/burst SKU architecture & memory safety plan

Jake —

Thanks again for the call today. Per our conversation, I ran a quick pass at a reserve + burst architecture that balances predictable throughput with cost-safe fallbacks for Vertex Labs' low-latency product APIs. Attaching a compact capacity worksheet (vertex_capacity_matrix.xlsx) with scenario rows; summary below.

High-level ask: can you confirm your 95th percentile token throughput target (tokens/sec) for production traffic and the percent of requests that will require >8k context? Those two numbers materially change the H100 vs A100 vs L4 split.

Recommendation summary (short):
- Reserve: a base pool of A100 nodes sized for steady-state concurrency and long-context work (memory-first). A100 provides the most predictable multi-GPU memory capacity per slot for Vertex's >8k requests.
- Burst: H100 GPUs for short bursts that are latency-critical and throughput-heavy. H100 performs better on FP16/TF32 workloads and reduces token cost on high-throughput tails.
- Edge/Cost-tier: L4 instances to serve cheap, short-context requests and embeddings where memory is not a blocker. Use prefix caching and an L4 quantized model to drive unit-cost down.

Tradeoffs to highlight:
- Memory headroom: A100 gives the best single-slot model memory without heavy tiling; if you have a large share of long-context calls (>8k tokens), A100 reduces KV-eviction risk.
- Throughput vs latency: H100 wins for end-to-end tokens/sec and batched throughput; A100 is steadier for memory-heavy single-reqs.
- Cost profile: L4 is orders of magnitude cheaper per token for short contexts; good for sampling/candidates and offloading non-critical workloads.

Attached: vertex_capacity_matrix.xlsx (scenario/slot math), and a short draft proposal PDF (reserve_burst_proposal_v1.pdf). Ben — I pinged you on the numbers we'd discussed for concurrency headroom; please add a quick ops-level table for failover and cache priming.

Next steps:
1) Jake: confirm 95p tokens/sec and % long-context mix.
2) Procurement: we'll provide a short path with reserve/burst counts and optional overage terms.
3) Ops: run a 48h pilot on mixed traffic to validate tail latency for H100 burst lanes.

—

Jake / Olga — dug into the worksheet and ran microbenchmarks against our internal models. Key operational notes below (ops-first perspective):

1) Recommended reserve mix for initial 6-month window (based on 42k 95p and 12% long-context):
   - A100 reserve: 12 slots (each slot = 4xA100-40GB equivalent tiling in our pool) — sized to handle the 12% long-context baseline with 20% headroom. Rationale: avoids frequent tiling/eviction and simplifies KV caching.
   - H100 burst pool: 6 nodes reserved as burst-capacity (on-demand-style billing) — tuned for batched throughput; we keep these as pre-warmed but metered.
   - L4 edge/economy: 10 L4 instances in a lower-tier pool for cheap short-context inference, embeddings, and reranking.

2) Failure/fallback behavior (answers your question #1):
   - If H100 runs out of KV for a long-context request, our smart routing will try an A100-compatible variant. That requires the model to be available in an A100-optimized format or to be sharded; otherwise the request will be queued/fail. In practice we recommend keeping canonical long-context model in A100 reserve and using H100 for throughput-optimized variants.

3) Commit recommendation (answers question #2):
   - Commit to A100 reserve as primary (predictable SLA and memory headroom).
   - For H100, we recommend a small committed pool (2-3 nodes) for the first quarter to reduce cold-start latency during peak windows; keep the remainder as burst (on-demand) to avoid overcommit.

4) Cost/ops tradeoffs:
   - A100 reserve increases predictable monthly spend but reduces latency risk on >8k requests.
   - H100 burst reduces average per-token cost on batched tails but introduces variability in availability — mitigated with 2-3 committed warm H100 nodes.
   - L4 pool is the best lever to reduce unit cost for non-long-context traffic; ensure strict routing rules and prefix caching for sessions.

5) Actionables for a 48h pilot:
   - Provision the reserve A100 12-slot baseline and 2 committed H100 warm nodes.
   - Mirror 10% of production traffic (sampling low-risk endpoints) to measure tail latency and KV eviction rates.
   - Capture per-token cost by route and run a quick billing estimate post-48h.

I attached a lightweight L4 memory benchmark summary (l4_memory-benchmark.pdf) and updated the reserve numbers into the worksheet.

Thanks for the quick turnaround and the clear numbers, Jake. Recap + procurement ask below so your finance team has a clean artifact to review.

Recap (decisions we recommend):
- Commit (6 months): A100 reserve = 12 slots (memory-first baseline).
- Commit (1 quarter): H100 warm = 3 nodes (to reduce peak cold-start SLA risk).
- On-demand / burst: additional H100 capacity (6 nodes) to be used as metered burst.
- L4: 10 instances (economy pool) with strict routing and prefix cache for short contexts.

Procurement line-item (rough monthly estimate):
- A100 12-slot reserve — estimated committed monthly: $86,000
- H100 3-node warm reserve — estimated committed monthly: $45,000
- H100 on-demand burst (metered) — variable (we'll cap at 20% of reserve spend for initial contract)
- L4 10 instances — estimated monthly: $6,500

Attachments: I pushed reserve_burst_proposal_v1.pdf with the above numbers and a short Overage policy clause (Cap at 20% by default; auto-alerts at 60% of cap). If this looks good, procurement@vertexlabs.com — please confirm route to PO and any special invoicing terms (net-45 is fine; if you need net-60 flag it early).
